name: The Authorship Rule
title: The Authorship Rule
answer: The Authorship Rule is a school's clear line for AI in student creative work: the student makes the work, and any AI help is disclosed. It matters because without it a student can submit an AI-generated image for an art assignment and think nothing is wrong. With it, teachers, students and families share the same expectation about authorship.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: The idea responds to a common confusion in creative subjects. A student may generate an image in seconds and hand it in as an art assignment, not realizing that this crosses a line. A clear rule removes that ambiguity by stating that the student is the author of the work. AI can still have a role, but only in defined ways and only when the student says so. The rule protects the meaning of creative work and gives everyone a shared reference point.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the rule permits AI for particular, bounded tasks. A student might use it to brainstorm ideas for a painting, locate reference images, or learn about an artist's methods. A layout tool such as Canva for Education or Adobe Express for Education can be used for a poster, provided the artwork and design choices remain the student's own. What is not allowed is presenting AI-made work as the student's creation. Figure 10.3 presents the rule in a form teachers can post and share with families, and the AI use levels from Chapter 3 fit here, with most creative assignments placed at the lower levels, while a few assignments may explore AI directly, such as comparing a student's drawing with an AI-generated one and discussing the differences, and those should be clearly labeled; for older students, the rule can connect to a discussion about copyright and what makes creative work belong to someone.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study or a research label for this rule. It cites UNESCO's guidance, which notes that the United States Copyright Office has said that output generated by AI is not protected by copyright, because copyright protects only work that comes from human creativity (Miao & Holmes, 2023). The text says this point makes a good discussion with older students. No other evidence or figure is given beyond Figure 10.3, which lays out the rule for teachers to post and share with families.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The rule sets limits so that AI cannot be presented as the student's own creation. It allows AI only in particular, bounded ways, such as brainstorming, finding reference images, learning about techniques, or using a layout tool, and only when the artwork and design choices are the student's own. Any AI help must be disclosed. The text notes a legal dimension: AI output is not protected by copyright because copyright protects human creativity. The decisions about what is allowed and what must be labeled stay with the school and teacher, and the student keeps authorship of the creative work.
